title: SHE SANG ABOUT GOD’S GOODNESS ON SUNDAY… THEN CRIED HERSELF TO SLEEP THAT NIGHT.
paragraphs: SHE SANG ABOUT GOD’S GOODNESS ON SUNDAY… THEN CRIED HERSELF TO SLEEP THAT NIGHT.

The congregation heard her worship. Heaven heard her weeping. And what Jesus does with the pain we hide behind our praise might change the way you understand faith, suffering, and the God who refuses to abandon His wounded children.
She was still wearing her Sunday dress when she finally broke down.
The same dress she had worn just hours earlier while standing beneath the church lights, holding a microphone, singing about the goodness of God.
People had raised their hands.
Some had closed their eyes.
Others had wiped away tears as her voice filled the sanctuary.
After the service, someone hugged her and said, “You are so anointed.”
Another whispered, “I wish I had faith like yours.”
She smiled.
She thanked them.
She even encouraged someone who had been struggling.
But nobody knew what was waiting for her when she got home.
Nobody knew how much strength it had taken just to stand on that platform.
Nobody knew that the woman singing about God's faithfulness was quietly wondering why her own life seemed to be falling apart.
And nobody knew that before midnight, the same voice that had led an entire congregation in worship would be trembling through a prayer she could barely finish.
“Lord… I know You're good.”
Silence.
“But why does everything hurt so much?”
If you have ever worshiped God publicly while privately wondering how much more pain you could endure, please keep reading.
Because there is something about Jesus that suffering people desperately need to understand.
And it may be the very thing you have been too exhausted to believe.
The woman in this story is a fictional portrait, but the struggle she represents is painfully real.
Perhaps her marriage was unraveling.
Perhaps bills were piling up on a kitchen table already covered with unanswered prayers.
Perhaps she had lost someone she loved, and everyone assumed she had recovered because she had stopped talking about it.
Perhaps depression had made ordinary mornings feel unbearably heavy.
Or perhaps there was no single catastrophe.
Just years of carrying everybody else's burdens while quietly neglecting her own wounds.
She was the dependable one.
The prayer warrior.
The woman who remembered birthdays, checked on sick church members, encouraged discouraged friends, and always seemed to have a Scripture ready.
She knew how to tell other people that God would make a way.
What she didn't know was how to admit that she was struggling to see one herself.
And that night, sitting on the edge of her bed, she finally whispered something she had been afraid to say aloud.
“God, I'm tired.”
Not tired from singing.
Not tired from church.
Tired from pretending that because she believed in God's goodness, she was never supposed to feel devastated.
Tired from answering “I'm blessed” when someone asked how she was doing.
Tired from being praised for her strength while secretly wishing someone would notice her exhaustion.
Tired from thinking that admitting her pain might somehow dishonor the God she loved.
And here is where this story becomes uncomfortable.
Because sometimes the very communities that proclaim God's healing can become places where wounded people feel pressured to hide their wounds.
Not necessarily because anyone intends to hurt them.
Sometimes because we have confused spiritual maturity with emotional invulnerability.
We celebrate the testimony after the breakthrough.
But what about the believer who is still waiting?
We applaud the person who declares victory.
But what about the Christian who can barely whisper, “Help me”?
We know what to do when someone says, “God answered my prayer!”
But do we know how to sit beside someone who says, “I have prayed for years, and I still don't understand”?
Somewhere along the way, many sincere believers began treating tears as evidence that faith was weakening.
Yet Scripture tells a remarkably different story.
And the difference matters.
In Psalm 13:1, David cries:
“How long wilt thou forget me, O LORD? for ever? how long wilt thou hide thy face from me?” (KJV)
The Hebrew opening is:
עַד־אָנָה יְהוָה
ʿAd-ʾānah YHWH
“How long, O LORD?”
These are not the words of an unbeliever mocking God.
They are the words of a man who knows God and is suffering deeply.
David does not conceal his anguish beneath religious language.
He brings it directly into the presence of the Lord.
He asks difficult questions.
He describes his sorrow.
And then, within the same psalm, he remembers God's steadfast love.
This is biblical lament.
Not the abandonment of faith, but suffering brought honestly before the One in whom faith rests.
The Hebrew Scriptures do not require hurting believers to pretend that their pain is imaginary.
They teach us to take our pain to God.
And perhaps someone reading this has spent years believing that honest sorrow and genuine worship cannot exist in the same heart.
But David's psalms show us otherwise.
A trembling voice can still pray.
A grieving heart can still trust.
A believer can have unanswered questions without surrendering the truth of God's character.
And a woman can sing about God's goodness on Sunday and cry herself to sleep that night without becoming a hypocrite.
Read that again.
Her tears did not automatically make her worship dishonest.
Her suffering did not prove that her faith was counterfeit.
Her exhaustion did not place her beyond the reach of God's mercy.
She might have been genuinely worshiping the Lord while desperately needing His comfort.
And if that sounds like you, there is something even more astonishing waiting in the Gospel of John.
Two sisters once sent word to Jesus that their brother was sick.
Mary and Martha loved Jesus.
Their brother Lazarus was loved by Jesus.
Yet Lazarus died.
When Jesus finally arrived, Martha spoke words that have echoed through centuries of grief.
“Lord, if thou hadst been here, my brother had not died.” (John 11:21, KJV)
Mary would later say essentially the same thing.
Think about the weight of that sentence.
They believed Jesus had power.
They knew He could heal.
But their brother was dead, and they were standing in the terrible space between what they believed Jesus could do and what He had allowed to happen.
Have you ever lived there?
Between God's power and your unanswered prayer?
Between what Scripture says about His goodness and what your circumstances seem to be screaming?
Between knowing He loves you and wondering why He has not changed what is breaking your heart?
Then notice what happens when Jesus sees Mary weeping.
John 11:35 records two words in English:
“Jesus wept.”
The Greek text reads:
ἐδάκρυσεν ὁ Ἰησοῦς
Edakrysen ho Iēsous.
“Jesus wept.”
The verb edakrysen describes Jesus shedding tears.
It is an extraordinary moment.
Jesus knows that He is about to raise Lazarus.
Yet He still weeps.
His knowledge of the coming resurrection does not make the present grief meaningless.
His divine authority does not make Him indifferent to human sorrow.
And His tears reveal something that suffering believers must never forget.
The Savior who has power over death is not emotionally detached from the people wounded by it.
Jesus does not stand at the tomb and rebuke Mary for crying.
He does not tell Martha that her sadness proves insufficient faith.
He enters the scene of their grief.
He is deeply moved.
He weeps.
Then He calls Lazarus from the grave.
This passage does not promise that every funeral will end with an immediate resurrection or that every tragedy will be reversed in this life.
It reveals Jesus as the resurrection and the life, the One whose victory over death reaches its fulfillment in the hope He gives to those who believe in Him.
But before the miracle at the tomb, there are tears.
And those tears matter.
Because the woman who sang on Sunday needs to know that her Savior understands what it means to weep.
So do you.
There is another moment in Scripture that takes this truth even deeper.
On the night before His crucifixion, Jesus enters Gethsemane.
The name Gethsemane is commonly connected with the idea of an oil press, a striking setting for the anguish that unfolds there.
Matthew 26:38 records Jesus saying:
“My soul is exceeding sorrowful, even unto death.”
The Greek expression includes:
περίλυπός ἐστιν ἡ ψυχή μου
Perilypos estin hē psychē mou.
“My soul is deeply sorrowful.”
The word perilypos conveys profound grief or distress.
Jesus is not pretending.
He is not performing sorrow to make a theological point.
He is facing the horror of what lies ahead.
He prays.
He submits Himself to the Father's will.
And He asks His disciples to remain with Him and watch.
Yet they fall asleep.
The disciples who had walked with Him, listened to Him, and witnessed His miracles could not remain awake in His hour of anguish.
Consider that for a moment.
The sinless Son of God experienced sorrow so deep that He described it as overwhelming.
Therefore, deep sorrow cannot, by itself, be evidence of personal sin or spiritual failure.
Jesus never sinned.
Yet Jesus grieved.
Jesus never lacked faith.
Yet Jesus experienced anguish.
And His submission to the Father was not the absence of pain.
It was obedience in the midst of it.
Hebrews 4:15 tells us that we have a high priest who can sympathize with our weaknesses, having been tempted as we are, yet without sin.
That does not mean Jesus experienced every circumstance exactly as we do.
It means our Savior is not distant, ignorant, or incapable of compassion.
He knows human suffering from within a truly human life.
And He is able to receive those who come to Him for mercy.
So perhaps the question is not, “Why am I crying if I really believe?”
Perhaps a better question is, “Why have I been so afraid to bring my tears to the Savior who wept?”
That Sunday night, our imagined worship leader sat with her Bible open.
Her makeup had been washed away.
Her phone was full of messages thanking her for the worship service.
She could barely bring herself to answer them.
She remembered someone saying, “You always seem so strong.”
And for the first time, she wished they had said something different.
“Are you okay?”
Not because she wanted attention.
Not because she wanted everyone to know her private struggles.
But because she was beginning to understand how lonely it can feel to be admired for a strength you are no longer sure you possess.
Maybe you know that loneliness.
Maybe you are the father who leads family prayer but secretly fears losing his job.
Maybe you are the mother who tells her children that Jesus loves them while struggling with grief no one else sees.
Maybe you are the pastor who has preached hope while carrying private exhaustion.
Maybe you are the young believer who sings with the worship team and then goes home to a house where there is more shouting than peace.
Maybe you are the person who keeps serving because you genuinely love Jesus, even though your heart has become dangerously weary.
And maybe, just maybe, you have mistaken your ability to keep functioning for evidence that you are healing.
They are not always the same thing.
You can fulfill your responsibilities while still needing help.
You can encourage other people while needing encouragement yourself.
You can know Scripture while struggling to apply its promises to your own suffering.
And you can love Christ sincerely while needing someone trustworthy to walk beside you.
God did not design the church to be a stage where everyone performs invulnerability.
The church is the body of Christ.
Galatians 6:2 says:
“Bear ye one another's burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ.”
Notice what this assumes.
Believers will have burdens.
And those burdens are not always meant to be carried alone.
Sometimes the next faithful step is not accepting another ministry assignment.
Sometimes it is admitting to a mature Christian friend, “I need prayer.”
Sometimes it is asking a pastor or counselor for help.
Sometimes it is seeking professional care for persistent depression, anxiety, trauma, or emotional distress.
Receiving appropriate care does not mean abandoning prayer or Scripture.
Nor should anyone be told to discontinue necessary medical treatment simply because they are seeking spiritual support.
God's people can pray, listen, encourage, provide practical assistance, and help someone access qualified care.
Spiritual maturity is not measured by how successfully we conceal our pain.
And a church that speaks constantly about grace should be a place where people can seek help without being shamed for needing it.
But there is an even deeper danger than hiding our pain.
It is allowing pain to distort what we believe about God.
When suffering continues, the heart begins asking questions.
“Did God forget me?”
“Am I being punished?”
“Does He love everyone else more?”
“Would He be more pleased with me if I were stronger?”
And sometimes those questions become accusations against ourselves.
We start searching for a hidden failure that might explain everything.
We assume that because our circumstances are difficult, God must be displeased.
But Scripture does not permit us to make that automatic conclusion.
Consider the man born blind in John 9.
The disciples asked Jesus whose sin had caused the man's blindness.
Jesus rejected the assumption that his condition could be explained by the personal sin of either the man or his parents.
That passage does not explain every instance of suffering.
But it warns us against confidently assigning blame where God has not revealed it.
Not every painful circumstance is divine punishment.
Not every delay is a spiritual rejection.
Not every illness is evidence of weak faith.
And not every season of sorrow means God has withdrawn His love.
At the same time, Scripture does call us to examine our hearts honestly.
There are wounds caused by other people's sins.
There are hardships that come from living in a fallen world.
And there are consequences of our own disobedience that require confession, repentance, and change.
Grace does not require us to deny these distinctions.
It requires us to bring the truth into the light.
If you have sinned, you do not need to defend it.
If you have been harmed, you do not need to pretend it was harmless.
If you are grieving, you do not need to manufacture a smile.
And if you are exhausted, you do not need to earn permission to seek help.
The Gospel is not an invitation to build a more convincing religious disguise.
It is an invitation to come to Jesus Christ in truth.
And this is where the story moves from sorrow to something far greater than temporary emotional relief.
Because Jesus did not come merely to make wounded people feel better about their circumstances.
He came to save sinners.
He came to reconcile us to God.
He came to bear our sins and conquer death.
Isaiah 53:5 says:
“But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed.”
In the Hebrew text, one central expression is:
וּבַחֲבֻרָתוֹ נִרְפָּא־לָנוּ
Uvaḥavurato nirpa-lanu.
“And by his wound, healing has come to us.”
In context, Isaiah 53 presents the suffering Servant bearing the sins and iniquities of others.
The New Testament explicitly connects this passage to Jesus Christ.
First Peter 2:24 applies this healing language to Christ's sin-bearing death and to believers turning from sin and living in righteousness.
Therefore, we must not reduce this verse to a guarantee that every physical or emotional wound will disappear immediately.
The healing secured through Christ is rooted in His saving work, bringing forgiveness, reconciliation, and ultimately the complete restoration promised in God's future.
That distinction does not weaken the promise.
It protects its true glory.
Jesus did not die merely to improve our circumstances.
He died to redeem us from sin and bring us to God.
And because He rose again, suffering and death do not have the final word for those who belong to Him.
This is why the cross matters to the woman who cries after church.
And to the man who cannot sleep.
And to the believer who feels spiritually numb.
And to the person whose past is full of decisions they wish they could undo.
The cross declares that our greatest hope is not found in pretending we are whole.
It is found in the crucified and risen Savior.
At Calvary, Jesus bore the judgment our sins deserved.
Through faith in Him, sinners receive forgiveness and reconciliation with God.
His grace does not excuse our rebellion.
It calls us out of it.
His mercy does not tell us that our sins were harmless.
It tells us that the Savior's sacrifice is sufficient for those who repent and trust Him.
And His resurrection assures us that redemption is not merely a beautiful religious idea.
It rests upon the living Christ.
The Greek word often translated “grace” is:
χάρις
Charis.
In passages such as Ephesians 2:8, it refers to God's gracious favor, by which salvation is given rather than earned.
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God.”
A gift.
Not a wage.
Not a reward for never crying.
Not a prize for maintaining a flawless Christian appearance.
Not a certificate presented to the person who managed to hide every weakness.
Salvation is God's gift through faith in Jesus Christ.
And this truth changes the way we understand spiritual growth.
We do not repent to purchase God's mercy.
We repent because the Gospel summons us to turn from sin and come to the Savior who is merciful.
We do not obey to make Christ's sacrifice sufficient.
We obey because the grace that saves us also teaches us to live differently.
We do not worship to prove that we have no pain.
We worship because Jesus is worthy, even when our hearts are hurting.
And sometimes the most sincere worship is not the song everyone hears.
Sometimes it is the prayer spoken through tears when no one is watching.
“Lord, I still believe. Help me where my faith is struggling.”
That prayer resembles the cry in Mark 9:24:
“Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief.”
The father who spoke those words did not present Jesus with a polished spiritual performance.
He brought his desperate need.
And Jesus responded with power.
That does not mean every struggling person will receive the exact outcome they desire.
But it does show that imperfect, dependent faith can bring its need to Christ.
You do not have to wait until you feel spiritually impressive to approach Him.
Come because He is merciful.
Come because He is Lord.
Come because He alone has the words of eternal life.
Come because His grace is greater than your ability to maintain appearances.
And if you have wandered into sin while trying to numb your pain, do not let shame convince you to remain there.
Bring that sin into the light.
Confess it.
Turn away from it.
Seek forgiveness and appropriate accountability.
Receive the mercy Christ promises to those who come to Him.
First John 1:9 says:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
There is no need to confuse emotional suffering with moral guilt.
But where real sin exists, there is no need to hide it either.
Jesus Christ is sufficient for the repentant sinner.
That is the scandal of grace.
Not that sin is unimportant.
But that the holy Son of God willingly gave Himself to rescue people who could never rescue themselves.
And that grace is powerful enough to begin transforming lives that seemed hopelessly tangled.
From hiding to confession.
From self-reliance to surrender.
From guilt to forgiveness.
From spiritual performance to honest dependence upon Christ.
Not because every earthly consequence disappears.
Not because every broken relationship is immediately restored.
Not because Christians are guaranteed an easy life.
But because Jesus changes our standing before God and begins making us new.
Second Corinthians 5:17 declares:
“Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.”
The promise is not that believers will never struggle again.
It is that union with Christ brings a genuinely new identity and life.
And the One who begins His good work in His people remains faithful.
Now imagine that woman again.
The church is empty.
The music has stopped.
The microphone has been put away.
No one is applauding.
She is sitting alone in her room.
Her tears have not magically disappeared.
Her financial situation has not necessarily changed.
Her grief has not suddenly vanished.
But something begins to shift as she reads the Scriptures.
She realizes that the Bible never commanded her to pretend.
She realizes that Jesus is not disgusted by the weakness she has been desperately trying to conceal.
She realizes that asking for help may be an act of humility rather than an admission of spiritual defeat.
And perhaps, for the first time in a long time, her prayer changes.
Instead of saying, “Lord, make me strong enough that nobody knows I'm struggling,” she whispers:
“Lord, teach me to trust You enough to stop hiding.”
The next morning, perhaps she sends a message to a trusted sister in Christ.
“I need someone to pray with me. I've been having a really difficult time.”
Maybe her friend calls.
Maybe they cry together.
Maybe they read a psalm.
Maybe they arrange to meet.
Maybe she finally receives the support she has needed for months.
Her story does not have to end with an instant miracle to reveal the faithfulness of God.
Sometimes grace meets us through Scripture.
Sometimes through repentance.
Sometimes through the kindness of another believer.
Sometimes through the courage to seek help.
Sometimes through endurance that would have been impossible without God's sustaining mercy.
And sometimes through the quiet assurance that even when our circumstances remain difficult, Christ has not ceased to be our Savior.
There is a verse that deserves to be remembered by everyone who has ever cried alone.
Psalm 56:8 says:
“Thou tellest my wanderings: put thou my tears into thy bottle: are they not in thy book?”
The Hebrew phrase is:
שִׂימָה דִמְעָתִי בְנֹאדֶךָ
Simah dimʿati venodekha.
“Put my tears in Your bottle.”
This is poetic language.
It is not a biblical claim that we should imagine God literally storing tears in physical bottles in heaven.
It is David's vivid appeal to the God who knows his suffering and does not treat it as insignificant.
His wanderings are known.
His tears are remembered.
His distress is not beyond God's attention.
And that is enough to make a wounded heart stop and consider something beautiful.
The tears you are ashamed of are not hidden from God.
The prayers you struggled to finish are not beyond His hearing.
The nights when you could not find the right words do not make you invisible to Him.
He knows.
And for those who belong to Christ, His love is not dependent upon their ability to maintain an appearance of strength.
Romans 8:38–39 declares that neither death nor life, nor the many powers and hardships named by Paul, can separate believers from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord.
That is not a promise of a trouble-free life.
It is a declaration of the security of God's love in Christ.
And perhaps that is the truth you need tonight.
Not that tomorrow will automatically be easier.
Not that every unanswered question will suddenly make sense.
Not that everyone who hurt you will apologize.
But that Jesus Christ remains Lord.
His Gospel remains true.
His grace remains sufficient.
His resurrection remains the foundation of Christian hope.
And your present sorrow does not have authority to rewrite who He is.
One day, according to Revelation 21:4, God will wipe away every tear from the eyes of His redeemed people.
Death will be no more.
Neither will mourning, crying, or pain.
That promise belongs to the final restoration God will bring, not to a guarantee that believers will experience no tears before then.
We still live in a world where Christians bury loved ones.
Where faithful people face illness.
Where families struggle.
Where injustice wounds.
Where grief can last much longer than anyone expected.
But we do not grieve as people whose only horizon is the grave.
Because Jesus Christ has risen.
And the resurrection means that the future of God's people is not ultimately determined by their darkest night.
Now I want to speak to the person who has been reading this while quietly thinking, “This is me.”
You do not have to write your entire story publicly.
You do not owe strangers the details of your trauma, marriage, illness, or private battles.
But perhaps you can take one honest step today.
Tell someone trustworthy that you need support.
Open the Scriptures without feeling pressured to pretend you are cheerful.
Pray, even if all you can say is, “Lord, have mercy.”
And if you are carrying guilt over sin, stop running from the One who calls sinners to repentance.
Jesus is not inviting you to decorate your chains.
He is calling you to Himself.
Or write “I'm still fighting” if, by God's grace, you are refusing to walk away from Christ.
Your experience may encourage someone who cannot yet imagine surviving what they are facing.
And if you are not ready to share anything personal, that is okay too.
You are not required to disclose your pain to prove your faith.
But please do not believe the lie that you must suffer completely alone.
And to the believers who are doing well right now, this message is for you too.
Look around your church.
Notice the person who always serves.
The woman who always smiles.
The man who always says he is fine.
The volunteer who never misses a Sunday.
The friend who has suddenly become quiet.
Do not assume that because someone is spiritually active, they are emotionally supported.
Sometimes the person who encourages everyone else is waiting for someone to ask a sincere question and remain long enough to hear the answer.
Reach out.
Listen without rushing to fix everything.
Pray without using Scripture to silence grief.
Offer practical help where you can.
And remember that kindness is not a substitute for truth, nor is truth an excuse for cruelty.
Jesus Christ is full of grace and truth.
His people should seek to reflect both.
If someone came to mind while you were reading, consider tagging them if doing so would encourage rather than embarrass them.
You might instead send this privately with a simple message:
“I thought of you while reading this. You don't have to explain anything, but I'm here if you need someone.”
Not because sharing a post earns God's favor.
Not because the reach of an article determines its spiritual value.
But because the people who need biblical encouragement are not always the ones who openly ask for it.
Some are quietly scrolling after a difficult day.
Some have stopped attending church because they feel ashamed.
Some have never understood that Christianity is centered on the grace of Jesus Christ rather than the perfection of religious people.
Some may be searching for a reason to open a Bible again.
Return to it on a night when you need to remember that lament is biblical, that Christ understands suffering, and that His grace does not depend upon your emotional performance.
Our desire is not merely to publish words that stir emotions for a moment.
It is to keep pointing people toward the living Word of God, the finished work of Jesus Christ, and the daily obedience of discipleship.
Because a powerful article cannot save a soul.
An emotional response cannot replace repentance and faith.
Jesus Christ alone saves.
And everything we build must remain beneath that truth.
That is also why we want to invite those who are able and willing to help sustain and expand this ministry.
Some believers may choose to make it part of their planned giving, alongside the tithes and offerings they give through their local church.
Second Corinthians 9:7 teaches that giving should be purposeful, voluntary, and cheerful, not compelled.
God is not glorified by manipulating people into financial decisions.
He is glorified when His people act in faith, truth, love, and willing generosity.
And if your household is facing financial hardship, please care for your essential responsibilities rather than feeling pressured to give beyond your means.
But if you have been blessed with the ability to support Gospel-centered ministry and believe in what we are doing, your partnership can help us continue and expand this work.
It can help us reach readers who are searching for answers, believers who need encouragement, and people who have never heard the Gospel explained clearly.
Those products are not substitutes for Scripture, the local church, or a living relationship with Christ.
The invitation is simple.
If this ministry is bearing good fruit in your life, consider helping us plant more seeds.
Not for applause.
Not for religious status.
Not because God needs our money.
But because the Gospel is worth proclaiming, Scripture is worth teaching, and people are worth serving in the name of Jesus Christ.
Before you leave, return with me one last time to that woman sitting alone in her Sunday dress.
Hours earlier, people had heard her sing.
They heard confidence in her voice.
They saw her raised hands.
They assumed they understood her story.
But later, behind a closed bedroom door, she was weeping.
And if we were writing a shallow story, this would be the moment when every problem disappeared.
Her phone would ring with miraculous news.
Every bill would be paid.
Every relationship would be healed.
Every prayer would receive the answer she wanted.
She would wake up smiling, and the story would end.
But real discipleship does not depend upon fictional guarantees.
Sometimes Monday arrives, and the hardship is still there.
Sometimes the diagnosis remains.
Sometimes the grief is still heavy.
Sometimes the marriage still needs counseling.
Sometimes the heart still aches.
And sometimes the most meaningful change is that a wounded believer finally stops confusing her pain with God's absence.
She opens her Bible again.
She reaches out for help.
She remembers the cross.
She remembers the empty tomb.
And she whispers:
“Jesus, I don't understand everything I'm going through. But I know You are my Savior. Teach me to follow You through this.”
That is not a promise that every tear will immediately stop.
It is a confession of faith in the One who has conquered sin and death.
And perhaps, next Sunday, she will sing again.
Maybe her voice will still tremble.
Maybe she will need to step away from the platform for a season and receive care.
Maybe she will discover that serving Jesus does not always mean holding a microphone.
Sometimes it means receiving the love and support of His people.
Sometimes it means sitting quietly in the congregation and allowing the words of Scripture to minister to her own soul.
Sometimes it means confessing sin and accepting accountability.
Sometimes it means learning to rest without believing she has failed God.
But whether she sings or sits, whether she smiles or weeps, the center of her hope remains the same.
Jesus Christ crucified.
Jesus Christ risen.
Jesus Christ sufficient.
Jesus Christ worthy.
And the grace of God that does not merely cover a painful past, but calls redeemed sinners into a transformed life.
So if you have been carrying a smile that hides a thousand tears, hear this invitation.
You do not have to keep pretending.
Bring your grief to the Lord.
Bring your sin to the cross.
Bring your questions to Scripture.
Bring your burdens into the care of trustworthy believers.
And place your ultimate hope not in the disappearance of every earthly struggle, but in the Savior who died and rose again.
Because the Christian story does not end at the grave.
And your story, if you belong to Christ, is held by the One who has promised a resurrection future beyond the reach of death.
Perhaps tonight you will still cry.
But your tears do not have to become your verdict on God's love.
The cross has already shown the costliness of that love.
The resurrection has already revealed the victory of your Savior.
And the Gospel is still calling you home.
The congregation heard the song she sang, but Jesus knew the tears she could not sing through.
